trading model.def: A mathematical rule that takes inputs observed now, such as past prices or volumes, and produces a prediction of some quantity at a later time.

feature.def: One of the inputs to a model: a number known at the time the prediction is made, such as yesterday's return or today's volume.

target.def: The quantity a model is trained to predict, observed after the prediction is made, such as the next day's return or its direction.

prediction horizon.def: How far ahead a model predicts: the time between the moment its features are observed and the moment its target is measured.

regression model.def: A model that predicts a continuous quantity, such as a return, a price or a volatility.

classification model.def: A model that predicts which of a finite set of categories an outcome falls into, such as up or down, usually with a probability for each.

lookahead bias.def: The error of letting a backtest use information that was not available at the moment of the decision, such as a figure before its publication date. It makes a backtest look better than any real trader could have done.

overfitting.def: Fitting a model so closely to its training data that it captures the noise as well as the signal. An overfitted model looks excellent in sample and predicts poorly on new data.

bias-variance tradeoff.def: The balance between two sources of error in an estimate: bias, being consistently wrong in one direction, and variance, the noise that comes from a finite sample. Complex models cut bias and add variance.

signal-to-noise ratio.def: The size of the predictable part of a quantity relative to its unpredictable part. For short-horizon returns it is very small, so the signal is hard to tell from chance.

neural network.def: A flexible model built from many layers of weighted sums passed through simple nonlinear functions. It can have thousands or millions of parameters, which makes it prone to overfitting noisy data.

residual.def: The gap between what a model predicted and what actually happened, for one observation.

cross-validation.def: Testing a model by fitting it on part of the data and scoring it on a part it was not fitted to, rotating through the data. The standard k-fold version splits the data at random, which leaks the future into training when the data are a time series.

walk-forward analysis.def: Testing a model on time series by training it only on data before each test period and scoring it on that period, then moving forward and repeating.

purged k-fold cross-validation.def: A version of cross-validation for financial time series, described by López de Prado (2018), that removes from training any observations whose targets overlap the test period.

in-sample.def: Measured on the same data a model was fitted to. In-sample performance is optimistic, because the fit has partly adapted to that data's noise.

out-of-sample.def: Measured on data a model was not fitted to, such as a later period. It is the honest estimate of how the model would have performed in real time.
